strengths: ORCA addresses a relevant problem: adapting pretrained visual representations to low-data robotic control without updating the diffusion backbone. Combining task-specific learned prompts with frame-dependent visual prompts is technically plausible and potentially useful.

Tables 1–3 report consistent improvements in suite-level averages across 12 tasks and three seeds. Relative to SCR, ORCA improves DMC from 68.3 to 74.3, MetaWorld from 90.4% to 95.2%, and Adroit from 58.0% to 65.3%, using only two to five demonstrations per task.

The component ablation provides evidence that the two prompt types work together: their combination achieves 74.3 on DMC, versus 69.8 for task prompts alone and 70.5 for visual prompts alone. Comparisons with textual prompts, CoOp, and TADP also make the experimental investigation more informative.

The manuscript clearly presents the overall motivation and architecture, includes attention visualizations and layer ablations, and reports inference costs rather than concealing the additional overhead.
weaknesses: The central benefit is not adequately isolated from the addition of DINOv2. ORCA introduces a second pretrained visual encoder and substantial trainable projection capacity, but there is no DINOv2-only policy or direct fusion of DINOv2 and SCR features. Table 4 demonstrates an interaction between prompts within ORCA, but cannot establish that diffusion conditioning is preferable to simpler uses of the additional representation. This is a material concern for attributing the reported gains to the proposed contribution.

There are consequential inconsistencies in the reported results. Table 6 labels t=0 as the default but reports a DMC mean of 70.8 and Reacher-easy score of 71.9, whereas Table 1 reports 74.3 and 87.6 for the stated default configuration. Figure 1 reports MetaWorld/Adroit means of 96.3/64.7, versus 95.2/65.3 in Tables 2–3. These differences are unexplained and weaken confidence in the experimental configuration and timestep conclusions.

The evaluation supports narrower claims than the manuscript makes. MetaWorld and Adroit report the best online success rates across periodic evaluations, without a clearly separate final evaluation or a specified rollout count. Three seeds and substantial variability do not establish significant improvements on every task; several results tie existing baselines. The claim of significant superiority across all 12 tasks is therefore unsupported.

The methodological originality and explanatory claims need stronger evidence. Learned diffusion prompts and conditioning through external visual encoders are acknowledged prior techniques, but the distinction from SD4Match and EcoDepth is not developed sufficiently. Moreover, selected attention maps do not establish domain gap as the cause of textual prompting failures. Static task captions are compared with frame-dependent visual conditions, without a controlled comparison separating conditioning modality, temporal specificity, and added encoder information.

Reproduction of the proposed modules remains underspecified: the DINOv2 variant, conversion of dense features into 16 visual tokens, projection architecture, feature-resolution alignment, and prompt-training hyperparameters are not adequately documented. The compression pseudocode also applies BatchNorm with hidden_dim after a convolution producing compress_dim channels. That code issue is readily correctable, but the missing architectural details are more substantial. Reported latency rises from 26 ms for SCR to 48 ms for ORCA, without hardware or training-cost context. Overall, the promising benchmark gains are outweighed by unresolved contribution attribution and experimental inconsistencies, rather than by the absence of real-world experiments alone.

strengths: ORCA addresses a relevant visual representation problem: adapting a frozen diffusion backbone to control tasks using behavior-cloning supervision. Combining learned task prompts with frame-specific visual prompts is a coherent and potentially useful approach.

Tables 1–3 report improvements over SCR across three benchmark suites: mean scores increase from 68.3 to 74.3 on DMC, 90.4 to 95.2 on MetaWorld, and 58.0 to 65.3 on Adroit. Evaluation covers 12 tasks with three seeds and reported standard deviations.

The component ablation supports using both prompt types: Table 4 reports 74.3 with both, versus 69.8 with task prompts alone and 70.5 with visual prompts alone. Layer and timestep ablations, explicit baseline captions, and attention visualizations provide additional analysis.
The appendix quantifies computational costs, reporting 48 ms latency versus 26 ms for SCR, and explains how discarding upsampling blocks reduces the diffusion backbone’s size.
weaknesses: The main comparison does not isolate the proposed conditioning mechanism from the additional DINOv2 representation and trainable projection capacity. There is no DINOv2-only policy or simple fusion of DINOv2 and SCR features. The prompt ablation establishes benefits within ORCA, but cannot establish whether diffusion conditioning is preferable to simpler ways of using the same visual information. This is consequential because the methodological novelty primarily combines existing prompting ideas for control.

Unexplained numerical discrepancies undermine confidence in the reported configuration. Table 6 labels its t=0 row as the default but reports a DMC mean of 70.8 and Reacher score of 71.9, versus 74.3 and 87.6 in Table 1. Figure 1 also reports MetaWorld/Adroit means of 96.3/64.7, versus 95.2/65.3 in Tables 2–3. These differences need reconciliation to interpret the main gains and ablations.

MetaWorld and Adroit report the best success rate across periodic online evaluations, without specifying an independent final evaluation or the number of evaluation episodes. Selecting maxima can inflate estimates. Three seeds provide some uncertainty information, but do not substantiate the claim of significant superiority across every task; several results tie baselines, including Drawer-open and Relocate.

The explanatory claims exceed the evidence. Selected cross-attention maps suggest grounding differences but do not establish domain mismatch as the cause of textual conditioning failures. Likewise, no dense-versus-global or frame-varying-versus-fixed visual-conditioning control directly tests the claimed need for fine-grained, dynamic prompts. Per-frame image conditioning alone does not establish temporal understanding.

Reproduction remains difficult despite the appendix: the DINOv2 variant, visual-token projection details, policy architecture, optimizer settings, and evaluation episode counts are not adequately specified. Separately, correctable presentation errors include inconsistent prompt notation around Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 applying BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution producing compress_dim channels.

Overall, the multi-suite gains and component analysis are worthwhile, and simulation-only evaluation is not itself grounds for rejection. However, the missing comparison controlling for the added visual encoder and the unresolved result discrepancies leave the central contribution insufficiently established. These concerns determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: ORCA addresses a useful problem: adapting pretrained visual representations to control tasks without updating the diffusion backbone. Combining learned task prompts with frame-dependent visual prompts is technically plausible and clearly motivated.

Tables 1–3 show improvements across three simulation suites with only two to five demonstrations per task. Relative to SCR, average performance increases from 68.3 to 74.3 on DMC, 90.4 to 95.2 on MetaWorld, and 58.0 to 65.3 on Adroit. Comparisons include both frozen representations and alternative conditioning approaches.

The component ablation supports combining the prompts: on DMC, task-only and visual-only conditioning achieve 69.8 and 70.5, respectively, versus 74.3 together. Layer-selection experiments and reporting results over three seeds provide additional empirical support.

The manuscript provides useful implementation information, full baseline captions, qualitative attention visualizations, and an explicit latency comparison. The approach could be useful for low-data visual imitation learning.
weaknesses: The main attribution remains unresolved. ORCA adds a pretrained DINOv2 encoder and substantial trainable projection capacity, but there is no DINOv2-only policy or direct fusion of DINOv2 and SCR features. Consequently, the experiments do not establish how much improvement comes specifically from diffusion conditioning rather than the additional representation and capacity. This matters because learned and image-derived diffusion prompts already appear in the cited SD4Match and EcoDepth work.

The evaluation reports the best success rates across periodic online evaluations for MetaWorld and Adroit, without describing independent held-out evaluation after checkpoint selection or the number of evaluation episodes. This can inflate estimates. Three seeds and substantial variability on several tasks also do not justify the claim of significant improvements across all 12 tasks; some results tie existing baselines.

Unexplained numerical discrepancies weaken confidence in the reported configuration. Table 6 labels t=0 as the default but reports a DMC mean of 70.8 and Reacher-easy score of 71.9, whereas Table 1 reports 74.3 and 87.6. Figure 1 also reports ORCA averages of 96.3 on MetaWorld and 64.7 on Adroit, differing from Tables 2–3.

The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Selected attention maps suggest grounding differences but do not establish that domain mismatch causes textual conditioning failures. There is also no dense-versus-global or matched-versus-shuffled visual-prompt ablation to substantiate the claimed importance of fine-grained, frame-specific information.

Reproduction is hindered by missing details about the DINOv2 variant, conversion of dense features into 16 visual tokens, policy architecture, and optimization settings. The compression pseudocode applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after producing compress_dim channels, an apparent implementation typo. Practical benefits also require qualification: reported inference latency is 48 ms versus 26 ms for SCR, and evaluation is confined to simulation.

Overall, the consistent benchmark gains and component evidence make this a worthwhile contribution, but the missing controls and unresolved evaluation/reporting issues leave the recommendation at the decision boundary.

strengths: ORCA provides a useful, technically plausible approach to adapting frozen diffusion representations for visual control: task-specific learned prompts and observation-dependent visual prompts are optimized through behavior cloning. Its contribution is primarily an effective integration and empirical study rather than a new prompting primitive.

The main experiments show consistent aggregate improvements across 12 tasks and three suites, with three-seed results and standard deviations. Relative to SCR, ORCA improves DMC from 68.3 to 74.3, MetaWorld from 90.4% to 95.2%, and Adroit from 58.0% to 65.3%. Comparisons against text prompts, CoOp, and TADP make the conditioning study informative.

The supplementary evidence meaningfully strengthens the submission: it includes DINOv2, SigLIP, and Theia baselines, alternative visual encoders, and three LIBERO-Long tasks. The LIBERO multi-task result improves from 23.3% for SCR to 46.6%, suggesting usefulness beyond the main single-task experiments.

The component ablation supports combining task and visual prompts: DMC averages are 69.8 and 70.5 with individual components versus 74.3 together. Comparisons with LoRA and RoboAdapter also address practical alternatives to full fine-tuning. Taken together, the supported empirical contribution favors acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The experiments do not fully isolate the proposed mechanism. ORCA adds a second pretrained encoder and trainable projection capacity, but there is no matched baseline that directly fuses DINOv2 and SCR features, nor a dense-versus-global visual-prompt comparison. The DINOv2-only and SD-VAE experiments partially address this concern, but do not establish that fine-grained conditioning is the decisive advantage over simpler feature integration.

The explanation for text-conditioning failure remains a hypothesis. Selected attention maps demonstrate associations, not that domain mismatch or incorrect grounding causes performance degradation. The evaluated captions are fixed per task, so the experiments also conflate linguistic conditioning with the absence of observation-specific information. Claims that dynamic visual conditions are necessary exceed what these comparisons establish.

Evaluation uses the best online success rate across periodically evaluated checkpoints for MetaWorld and Adroit, without describing independent checkpoint selection and final testing. This can produce optimistic estimates. Three seeds and sometimes substantial variance also do not support the claim of significant superiority across all 12 tasks: ORCA ties several baselines, including CLIP on Relocate and all methods on Drawer.

Important reproduction details remain unspecified, including optimizer settings, policy architecture, precise visual-token projection and spatial reduction, feature-map alignment before concatenation, and the LIBERO training and task-conditioning protocol. The compression pseudocode applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution producing compress_dim channels, which is inconsistent when these dimensions differ.

Efficiency and deployment claims need qualification. Table F reports 48 ms latency versus 26 ms for SCR and 11 ms for VC-1, without hardware or timing protocol details. Freezing the backbone reduces task-specific parameter storage, but does not establish low training cost because gradients must propagate through it to train prompts. Evaluation remains entirely simulated.

There are correctable reporting inconsistencies: Figure 1 gives ORCA means of 96.3% and 64.7% for MetaWorld and Adroit, whereas Tables 1–2 give 95.2% and 65.3%; some standard deviations differ between Tables 1 and 4. Prompt symbols around Equation 3 are confused, and the Figure 6 discussion is duplicated. These issues do not negate the results, but reduce confidence in reporting precision.

strengths: ORCA provides a useful, technically plausible approach to adapting frozen diffusion representations for visual control: jointly learning task tokens and image-dependent visual prompts through behavior cloning. The empirical contribution supports weak acceptance despite limited methodological novelty and reservations about experimental reporting.

Tables 1–2 show consistent aggregate improvements over the closely related SCR baseline: 68.3 to 74.3 on DMC, 90.4 to 95.2 on MetaWorld, and 58.0 to 65.3 on Adroit. Results include three seeds and standard deviations, and comparisons against text conditioning, CoOp, and TADP help establish the usefulness of the proposed combination.

The ablations provide meaningful support beyond benchmark rankings. Table 4 shows that combining task and visual prompts outperforms either alone on average. Table C demonstrates benefits using SD-VAE features without an external vision encoder, partially addressing whether improvements simply come from adding DINOv2.

The supplementary evaluation adds stronger representation baselines, three LIBERO-Long tasks with single-task and multitask results, and latency measurements. Comparisons with LoRA and RoboAdapter also make the evaluation more informative than comparisons solely against frozen encoders.
weaknesses: The distinctive mechanism is incompletely isolated. Learned prompting and visual conditioning of diffusion models already appear in the cited literature, making the main novelty their combination and application to control. There is no matched comparison against directly fusing DINOv2 and SCR features, nor a controlled dense-versus-global visual-prompt ablation. Consequently, the experiments establish the effectiveness of the system more clearly than the necessity of its particular conditioning design.

The evaluation protocol limits confidence in the reported performance estimates. Section 6.1 reports the best success rates among periodic online evaluations for MetaWorld and Adroit, without clearly describing independent final evaluation or the number of evaluation episodes. Selecting the maximum can produce optimistic estimates. Three seeds provide useful uncertainty information, but do not substantiate the claim of a significant margin across every task: several results are tied or differ only slightly.

The explanation for textual conditioning failures is suggestive rather than established. Selected attention maps do not demonstrate that domain mismatch causes the performance changes. The tested captions are fixed task descriptions, whereas ORCA receives frame-dependent visual information and action-supervised adaptation. Thus, the evidence supports limitations of these particular text baselines, rather than a general conclusion that textual conditions are ineffective for robotic control.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript specifies demonstrations, epochs, prompt lengths, and feature layers, but omits important optimizer settings, policy architecture details, visual-token projection specifications, and sufficient LIBERO training and conditioning details. Algorithm 1 also applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution producing compress_dim channels, which is inconsistent as written. This appears readily correctable, but the supplied pseudocode cannot be followed literally.

Some claims and presentation details need correction. Figure 1 reports ORCA suite means that disagree with Tables 1–2, and the Figure 6 discussion is duplicated. The claimed minimal overhead also needs qualification: Table F reports 48 ms latency versus 26 ms for SCR and 11 ms for VC-1, without measurement hardware or batch settings. These issues do not erase the measured gains, but weaken clarity and practical efficiency claims.

strengths: ORCA makes a useful contribution to visual representation learning for control: task-specific learned prompts and frame-specific visual tokens adapt a frozen diffusion backbone through behavior cloning. The approach is straightforward, and retaining a shared backbone while storing task-specific prompting modules has practical value.

The main experiments support improvements across three distinct control suites. Relative to SCR, ORCA improves mean DMC score from 68.3 to 74.3, MetaWorld success from 90.4% to 95.2%, and Adroit success from 58.0% to 65.3% (Tables 1–2). Reporting three seeds and standard deviations helps assess variability.

The component ablation provides meaningful support for combining the prompts: on DMC, task prompts alone achieve 69.8 and visual prompts alone achieve 70.5, while their combination reaches 74.3 versus the 68.3 baseline (Table 4). Comparisons with text prompts, CoOp, TADP, and parameter-efficient adaptation strengthen the experimental argument.

The supplement substantially extends the evidence with DINOv2, SigLIP, and Theia baselines, alternative visual encoders, timestep ablations, efficiency measurements, and three LIBERO-Long tasks under single-task and shared-policy training. The SD-VAE prompting variant also improves performance without an external visual backbone.

Overall, the consistent benchmark-level gains and complementary ablations provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection. The contribution is primarily empirical and architectural, but it is relevant and sufficiently supported for a weak accept.
weaknesses: The experiments do not fully isolate conditioning from feature fusion and additional capacity. ORCA adds a visual encoder and 10.6M trainable parameters, but there is no matched baseline that directly combines DINOv2 and SCR features at the policy input. DINOv2-only results and the SD-VAE ablation partially address this concern, but do not establish that routing visual information through diffusion conditioning is preferable to simpler fusion.

Evaluation uses the best success rate across periodic online evaluations for MetaWorld and Adroit (Section 6.1). Without a separately reported held-out evaluation after checkpoint selection, this introduces selection optimism. The number of evaluation episodes is unspecified, and three seeds with substantial variability on some tasks do not support the blanket claim of significant improvement across all 12 tasks. Several outcomes are ties.

Reproducibility is incomplete: optimizer settings, learning rates, policy architecture, image preprocessing, and the precise visual-token projection are insufficiently specified. Figure 4 marks the vision encoder as learnable, whereas Appendix A.6 describes DINOv2 as frozen. The compression pseudocode also applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution producing compress_dim channels, which would fail when those dimensions differ.

The explanation for textual conditioning failures is plausible but not established causally. Selected attention maps and comparisons with fixed task captions cannot distinguish domain mismatch from caption quality, insufficient state information, or prompt formulation. Likewise, the claimed importance of dense, frame-sensitive prompts lacks direct pooled-feature and static-versus-changing visual-prompt controls.

Originality is moderate because learned prompts and visual conditioning of diffusion representations already appear in the cited SD4Match, EcoDepth, and TADP literature. The strongest novelty is their application and empirical validation in control. Evidence remains simulation-based, and the small LIBERO subset does not establish broad language-conditioned generalization.

Efficiency and reporting claims need qualification. Table F reports 48 ms latency versus 26 ms for SCR and 11 ms for VC-1, without hardware or batch-size details; parameter-efficient adaptation therefore does not imply negligible runtime overhead. Separately, correctable reporting inconsistencies include Figure 1's MetaWorld/Adroit means of 96.3/64.7 versus 95.2/65.3 in Tables 1–2, differing standard deviations for repeated results, and duplicated discussion of Figure 6.
